subtopic: Drawn into a high-control group or online extremism
passage:
Jyoti: you missed Mitali's birthday again. she asked about you
Ankita: I had the evening session
Ankita: honestly I can't do those parties anymore. they're so empty
Jyoti: empty? that's us you're talking about
Ankita: I don't mean you exactly. I mean the whole way people live
Ankita: the group says most people are asleep. you just can't see it from inside
Jyoti: and your mum and dad? are they asleep too?
Ankita: they're part of the system. they'd never understand
Jyoti: Ankita, you're his only daughter. your dad drove four hours to bring you home when you were sick last year
Ankita: see, this is exactly what they said would happen
Ankita: people outside try to pull you back with guilt
Jyoti: I'm not trying to pull you anywhere. I'm just worried about you
Ankita: that's what they all say
Jyoti: ok. I'm still here, whenever you want

qa.q: Whose birthday did Ankita miss again?
What does Ankita now believe about people outside the group, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ankita calls ordinary friends' parties empty, calls her parents part of the system, and treats Jyoti's worry as outside pressure.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that keeps a turning point open for Ankita later?
qa.a: Jyoti stayed calm, didn't attack the group, and said she would still be there, so Ankita has a safe person to come back to.

qa.q: What is it like for Jyoti when that concern is called 'what they all say'?
qa.a: Jyoti feels shut out and hurt, as if her real care has been turned into proof against her.

grounding: It shows a young woman beginning to see outsiders, parents and friends as blind or hostile, and reading a friend's worry as outside influence.

passage:
In the kasba, everyone knew the new centre above the cloth shop on Station Road. Swati had started going in January, for 'personality classes'. By April she was going every evening.
On the veranda one night her father asked why she'd stopped helping at the shop. Swati, nineteen, looked at him with a strange calm. 'You think small, Papa. Everyone in this town does. They're scared of real change.'
When Yogesh, her friend since primary school, met her at the bus stand and asked, carefully, what they actually taught there, she said, 'You wouldn't understand. You're still inside the old thinking.'
'Swati, I'm just asking.'
'That's how it starts. Questions. They told us people would try.'
She did have doubts some nights. She'd lie awake, remembering her mother's face. But at the centre they said doubt was weakness, the town's voice in your head. So in the morning she pushed it away.

qa.a: It was above the cloth shop on Station Road.

qa.q: What does Swati feel when her doubts come at night?
qa.a: She feels unsettled, remembering her mother's face, but has learned to see doubt as weakness and pushes it away.

qa.q: What could Yogesh or Swati's family do that might help at this stage?
qa.a: They could stay warm and in touch without arguing about the centre, and gently seek advice from a counsellor or trusted elder on how to support her.

qa.q: How might Swati's father feel after being told he thinks small?
qa.a: He may feel hurt and bewildered, sensing his daughter slipping away and not knowing how to reach her.

grounding: It shows a young woman beginning to see her town, parents and old friend as blind or hostile, with her own doubts treated as weakness.
